Juvenile red drum (Sciaenops ocellatus) exhibit rapid growth during their first year, with individuals reaching a total length at puberty of 68 centimeters [Lp = 68 centimeters], typically occurring within a range of 66 to 70 centimeters depending on local environmental conditions. This milestone marks the onset of gonadal development and the transition from an immature, purely somatic growth phase to one where reproductive tissues begin to mature. The timing of this transition is closely linked to water temperature, and under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at a stable 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since birth at puberty is approximately 1,460 days [tp = approximately 1,460 days]. This relatively protracted juvenile period, spanning several years, is characteristic of long-lived sciaenids and reflects a life-history strategy that prioritizes the accumulation of substantial body reserves before the energetic demands of spawning commence. Field studies from the Gulf of Mexico corroborate this estimate, though some variation is observed across latitudinal gradients, with faster maturation reported in warmer, more productive estuaries where prey is abundant throughout the year.

Fecundity in this species is remarkably high, a trait common among marine broadcast spawners that produce large numbers of small, pelagic eggs. At a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], each reproductive female releases approximately 9,589 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 9,589 eggs per day], a rate that accumulates over the extended spawning season, which can last for several months. This daily output is achieved through a combination of high clutch frequency and substantial batch fecundity; individuals may spawn every 2 to 4 days during the peak of the season, resulting in an annual fecundity that can reach into the millions of eggs. The production of such a vast number of offspring is an energetically costly endeavor, and gravid females exhibit a noticeable increase in their condition factor just prior to the spawning period, drawing on lipid stores accumulated during the preceding autumn. The reproductive rate at this temperature is among the highest documented for any sciaenid of comparable size, highlighting the species' capacity for rapid population recovery under favorable thermal regimes.

The initial wet weight at birth is remarkably low, with newly emerged yolk-sac larvae weighing only 0.00053 grams [Wwb = 0.00053 grams], a value derived from an egg diameter of approximately 1.0 millimeter. This minuscule size places the larvae squarely within the ichthyoplankton community, where they are subject to intense predation pressure and must begin exogenous feeding within days of hatching to avoid starvation. The yolk-sac larvae are entirely lecithotrophic during the first few days post-eclosion, relying on endogenous reserves while their mouthparts and digestive systems complete differentiation. The transition to exotrophic feeding marks a critical bottleneck in the early life history, and survival during this period is heavily contingent upon the spatial and temporal overlap with adequate concentrations of suitable zooplankton prey, particularly copepod nauplii and rotifers, which must be present in the water column at the moment of first feeding onset.

As red drum approach their maximum size, they attain a truly impressive body mass. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult can reach 45,000 grams [Wwi = 45,000 grams], representing one of the largest asymptotic masses recorded among western Atlantic sciaenids. Achieving this size requires a sustained period of somatic growth that may span two decades or more, with individuals continuing to add both length and mass well after reaching sexual maturity. In parallel with this increase in mass, the total length of the largest individuals—those that have completed the majority of their somatic growth—can reach 115 centimeters [Li = 115 centimeters]. However, a more typical ultimate total length for many populations is closer to 100 centimeters [Li = 100 centimeters], with the discrepancy likely reflecting regional differences in prey availability, fishing pressure, and thermal regimes. These dimensions place the species among the apex predators of shallow estuarine and nearshore ecosystems, where large adults feed primarily on blue crabs, penaeid shrimp, and various finfish.

The wet weight at puberty represents an energetic threshold that marks the transition from somatic growth to reproductive investment. Field data indicate that individual red drum typically attain a wet weight of approximately 3,700 grams [Wwp = approximately 3,700 grams] at the onset of gonadal maturation, with most estimates falling within a range of 3,400 to 4,000 grams depending on local food web dynamics. This body mass threshold ensures that individuals have accumulated sufficient energy reserves to support the substantial metabolic costs associated with gamete production and spawning migrations. Under the thermal conditions typical of their native range (25 °C [T = 25 °C]), the maximum life span is estimated at approximately 60 years [am = approximately 60 years], a remarkable longevity that is comparable to that of some deepwater rockfishes and emphasizes the species' slow pace of life relative to its high fecundity. This extended life span allows for multiple reproductive episodes across decades, reinforcing an iteroparous breeding strategy in which older, larger individuals contribute disproportionate numbers of offspring to the next generation, thereby buffering the population against years of poor recruitment.
